children: Almonty Industries, a leading global producer of tungsten concentrate, has signed a binding agreement with the Government of Rwanda. Under the terms of the agreement, Kigali will receive a 25 percent interest in Almonty Rwanda Ltd in exchange for contributing the Shyorongi exploration concession and a mineral processing permit.
This partnership was introduced by the US Department of State under the 2025 US-Rwanda Framework for Shared Economic Prosperity.
The agreement also enables Almonty Rwanda, with government assistance, to purchase ore, pre-concentrate, and panning tailings from Rwandan mining licence holders for sale or upgrading.
Almonty Rwanda intends to export this material until a collection and processing plant is built in Rwanda.
This gives the partnership access to material from Rwanda's existing production base in the near term rather than depending on future exploration at Shyorongi.
Rwanda is the only African country among the world's 10 largest tungsten producers to sign this kind of deal.
The deal is designed to combine three elements of the sector on a single platform: the acquisition and upgrading of ore, pre-concentrate, and panning tailings from Rwandan mining licence holders.
This agreement is the first step towards a more comprehensive investment and development framework with the government, covering future investment and development in Rwanda.

Lewis Black, Almonty's Chief Executive Officer, said: “The most immediate opportunity is the material already being produced. Rwanda's small-scale licence holders are producing ore, pre-concentrate and panning tailings. This agreement allows us to collect, upgrade and export that material while we build out the collection and processing plant.”Alice Uwase, CEO of the Rwanda Mining Board, said that the country is happy to welcome Almonty as a strategic partner in the development of the tungsten industry.“This investment will help to transform our mining sector by introducing world-class processing infrastructure, international standards for environmental and social governance, and a comprehensive training programme to develop Rwandan talent,” she said.
She added that the partnership advances the country’s vision of establishing a modern, sustainable mining industry that will create lasting value for Rwandan people.
However, Rwanda has been accused of trading in conflict minerals smuggled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, which has raised doubts about the traceability of its minerals.

The US Department of the Treasury has sanctioned the Rwanda Gasabo gold refinery, accusing Kigali of facilitating the laundering and processing of millions of dollars worth of conflict gold smuggled from rebel-held areas in eastern DRC.

The M23 rebels, who are fighting the DRC government and are believed to be supported by Rwanda, have captured and controlled vast mineral-rich territories, fuelling speculation that they are colluding with Rwanda to smuggle minerals.
In 2024, Rwanda earned between $1.7 and $1.75 billion from mineral exports, driven heavily by gold and the ‘3Ts’ (tin, tungsten and tantalum).

Gold contributed approximately $1.5 billion (88.2 percent of total mineral earnings) in 2024, while tin (cassiterite), tungsten (wolfram) and tantalum (coltan) remain critical minerals that are fundamental to global electronics and technology supply chains.
